title: TDD — Red, Green, Refactor
summary: Test-driven development is a design technique wearing a testing costume — writing the test first forces a usable API to exist before the implementation does. Learn the red-green-refactor loop and when it's actually worth the discipline.

slides.markdown:
Everything so far in this group — [unit testing principles](unit-testing-principles), [test doubles](test-doubles-mocking) — assumed the code already exists and you're testing it after the fact. **TDD flips the order**: you write a failing test for behavior that doesn't exist yet, write just enough code to pass it, then clean up, and repeat.

The common misconception is that TDD is about test coverage. It isn't, primarily — it's a **design technique**. Writing the test first forces you to decide what a usable, callable interface looks like before you've committed to any implementation, which is a genuinely different discipline than writing code and testing it afterward. This topic is the loop itself, the two schools of applying it, and when the discipline earns its cost.

slides.subTitle: Red, then green, then refactor
slides.markdown:
The cycle has three strict phases, repeated for every small piece of behavior:

1. **Red** — write a test for behavior that doesn't exist yet. Run it. It must fail — if it passes immediately, either the behavior already existed or the test isn't actually testing anything.
2. **Green** — write the smallest amount of implementation code that makes the test pass. Not the best code, not the general solution — the minimum.
3. **Refactor** — with the safety net of a passing test, clean up the implementation (and the test, if needed) without changing behavior. Remove duplication, improve names, extract structure.

Then the cycle repeats for the next small piece of behavior. Each iteration is meant to be minutes, not hours — a red-green-refactor cycle that takes half a day has stopped being TDD in any meaningful sense; it's just testing after the fact with extra ceremony.

Writing the test first means writing the **call site** before the implementation — `parser.parse("3 + 4")` has to exist and look reasonable before `parse` has a single line of body. This forces an early, concrete answer to questions that are easy to defer indefinitely when writing implementation first: what arguments does this take, what does it return, what does the caller actually need versus what feels natural to expose from the inside.

The practical effect: TDD tends to produce smaller, more focused units, because a test that's painful to set up — needing five mocked dependencies just to call one method — is immediate, uncomfortable feedback that the design itself has a problem, *before* you've built anything around that design. Code written implementation-first doesn't get that signal until someone tries to test it later, by which point the awkward shape is already load-bearing elsewhere in the codebase.

| | Outside-in (acceptance-driven) | Inside-out (unit-first) |
|---|---|---|
| Starts with | A high-level acceptance test for the whole feature | A low-level unit test for the smallest building block |
| Direction | Works inward, mocking collaborators that don't exist yet | Works outward, composing tested units into larger behavior |
| Discovers the design | Top-down — the API shape emerges from what the feature needs | Bottom-up — the API shape emerges from what's easy to build correctly |
| Risk | The acceptance test can stay red for a long time while inner pieces are built | Can build well-tested units that don't actually compose into the needed feature |

Outside-in suits features with a clear user-facing behavior to anchor on — you know what "done" looks like from outside, and TDD discovers the internals needed to get there. Inside-out suits building a well-understood, reusable component (a parser, a data structure) where the internal correctness is the main risk. Many teams blend both: an outside-in acceptance test for the feature, inside-out unit tests for the pieces it decomposes into.

slides.subTitle: FizzBuzz, a few cycles in
Why that constraint matters
slides.markdown:
The green step's rule — write the least code that makes the test pass, not the general or "correct" solution — feels counterintuitive at first, and even a little silly in the FizzBuzz walkthrough. But it's doing real work: it forces every generalization in the code to be driven by an actual failing test demanding it, rather than by a guess about what might be needed later.

The failure mode it prevents is over-engineering ahead of evidence — writing a fully general, configurable solution for a problem you've only seen one example of, based on an assumption about future requirements that may never materialize. TDD's discipline is: **the tests are the source of truth for what the code needs to do**, and the implementation should never be more general than what's currently demonstrated necessary. Extra generality that isn't demanded by a test is a design decision made without evidence.

slides.subTitle: When writing tests first actually changes the design
slides.markdown:
| | TDD (test-first) | Test-after |
|---|---|---|
| When the test is written | Before the implementation exists | After the implementation is written |
| Design feedback | Immediate — an awkward test signals an awkward design before it's built | Late or absent — the design is already fixed by the time tests are written |
| Coverage tendency | Naturally high, since every behavior started as a test | Depends on discipline; easy to skip "obvious" cases after the fact |
| Risk of testing implementation details | Lower — the test was written against behavior, not against code that already exists to peek into | Higher — tempting to test whatever the code happens to do internally |

The honest case for TDD isn't "more tests get written" — a disciplined engineer can write thorough tests after the fact too. It's that test-first surfaces design problems (five-argument constructors, painful setup, hidden dependencies) **while they're still cheap to fix**, before any other code has been built on top of the awkward shape.

slides.sectionTitle: Over-specifying implementation, killing the refactor step
slides.markdown:
The refactor step only works if tests check **behavior** (inputs and outputs) rather than **implementation** (which internal method was called, in what order). A test written as `assert calculate_total.called_with(items, discount=0.1)` — asserting the exact internal call shape — breaks the moment you refactor `calculate_total`'s internals, even if the observable result is identical.

When this happens across a codebase, refactoring stops being safe: every internal restructuring, even a pure rename, triggers a wave of test failures unrelated to any actual behavior change. Teams respond, rationally but wrongly, by refactoring less — the tests meant to enable safe change have become the thing preventing it.

The fix is the same principle from [Unit Testing Principles](unit-testing-principles): assert on observable outputs and state, reserve interaction assertions for cases where the interaction genuinely has no other observable trace, as covered in [Test Doubles & Mocking](test-doubles-mocking).

TDD's cost is real: it slows down the first pass through a problem, in exchange for design feedback and a regression safety net. That trade isn't always worth making.

- **Throwaway spikes.** Code written purely to answer "is this approach even feasible," intended to be deleted regardless of outcome, gains nothing from a design discipline aimed at long-lived correctness.
- **Exploratory UI work.** When you genuinely don't know what the interface should look like yet and are iterating visually, writing tests against a design that will change wholesale in an hour is pure overhead.
- **Deeply unfamiliar problem spaces.** If you can't yet articulate what "correct" looks like — a novel algorithm, an unfamiliar domain — writing a test first means guessing at a specification you don't actually have yet.

The senior-level read: TDD is a tool for building something you understand well enough to specify, incrementally, with confidence. Where that understanding doesn't exist yet, prototype first, then apply TDD once the shape of the real solution is clear.

slides.subTitle: Triangulation and the transformation priority premise
slides.markdown:
Two disciplines separate reflexive TDD practice from genuine fluency. **Triangulation** is writing multiple test cases before generalizing an implementation, specifically to force a general solution rather than one that happens to satisfy a single example — the FizzBuzz walkthrough's cycle 2 (only handling 3) versus cycle 3 (generalizing once 5 was also demanded) is triangulation in miniature.

The **transformation priority premise** is a more formal idea: at each green step, prefer the *smallest* code transformation that makes the test pass — from "return a constant" to "return a variable" to "add a conditional" to "add a loop" — rather than jumping straight to a general recursive or iterative solution. Following this ordering tends to produce implementations that emerge naturally from the tests, rather than ones where the developer has silently pre-decided the final shape and is just writing tests to justify a solution already in their head — which defeats the entire premise of test-first design discovery.

slides.sectionTitle: TDD and the rest of the testing pyramid
slides.markdown:
TDD is a **workflow for writing tests**, not a statement about which layer of the [test pyramid](testing-fundamentals-pyramid) they belong to — it's most naturally applied to fast, isolated unit tests, since the red-green-refactor loop depends on tests running in seconds, but the same discipline scales to integration tests where the feedback loop tolerates being slower.

What TDD does **not** replace: [integration and e2e tests](integration-testing) covering the seams TDD's fast inner-loop tests structurally can't reach — a real database's actual behavior, a real third-party API's real response shape. A codebase built entirely test-first at the unit level can still ship a broken integration if nothing ever exercises the real boundary, which is exactly the risk [test doubles](test-doubles-mocking) covered under over-mocking.

TDD's inner loop is deliberately narrow — fast, isolated, one behavior at a time. The next topic, **Integration Testing**, is about the tests that verify what TDD's fast loop structurally can't: that a unit actually behaves correctly against its real collaborators, not just against the doubles standing in for them.
